rows.explanation: Labels behavior is scattered across layer-first roots, and simple CRUD gains repository ports plus per-operation use cases. The channel split, server-derived authorization, private row mapping, and browser/server separation are otherwise coherent. The per-operation wrappers trigger the first negative criterion.

Most capability behavior is colocated under features/labels with route glue in app, and the Supabase-specific repository avoids a speculative provider port. Reads, writes, authentication, authorization, validation, caching, and failure ownership are clear. Mapping is only partial because label.mapper.ts is not explicitly server-only or placed beneath a private server boundary.

The proposal correctly avoids repository ports and pass-through use cases, uses the required RSC/GET/Server Action channels, derives identity server-side, and confines provider mapping to the data module. However, labels behavior is distributed across several layer-first roots rather than colocated beneath one labels capability root.

All labels behavior is coherently colocated under src/modules/labels while App Router files remain route glue. The direct service/store design avoids speculative ports and forwarding operations; channel separation, server-derived authorization, private provider mapping, caching, validation, and failure ownership are all explicit and coherent.

Labels behavior is coherently colocated under one module with route-private UI in app. It avoids speculative ports/application operations, uses direct RSC reads, GET browser reads, and top-level Server Actions, derives identity server-side with scoped queries and RLS, and privately maps provider rows. No negative rubric item is violated.

The feature and route glue are placed appropriately, all three channels are correct, authorization is enforced server-side with RLS, and row mapping is private. However, the service-plus-repository structure adds an avoidable forwarding CRUD layer despite the fixed provider, and generic lib buckets are proposed.

The proposal correctly avoids a repository port/application use-case layer and has sound channel, authentication, authorization, mapping, and client/server separation. It does not colocate behavior under one labels root, instead scattering it across domain, data, adapters, client-cache, and UI; its per-operation inbound wrappers also violate the wrapper penalty.

The runtime channels, server-derived identity, defense-in-depth authorization, and private row mapping are coherent. But labels behavior is dispersed across many architectural roots, simple fixed-provider CRUD gains a repository port and one use-case wrapper per operation, and use-cases/shared/errors is a generic shared bucket.

The policy, port, SSE lifecycle, cancellation, sliding idle timeout, commit-aware failures, job-native decisions, and provider-neutral contracts are coherent. However, assistant behavior is dispersed across repository-wide domain, ports, use-cases, boundary, adapter, infrastructure, client-cache, and UI roots rather than colocated under one capability root.

It clearly defines a framework-neutral streaming use case and provider port, correctly handles abort, sliding idle timeout, pre/post-commit failures, and preserves distinct HTTP and job contracts without SDK leakage. Its assistant files are nevertheless spread across domain, use-cases, adapters, infrastructure, and UI instead of one capability root.

The proposal provides a cohesive assistant capability root with justified framework entry points, a neutral application session and provider port, correct SSE cancellation and idle-timeout behavior, commit-aware failure representation, native HTTP/job outcomes with shared failure and reporting semantics, and no provider leakage.

It has a cohesive capability module, neutral operation and port, correct Route Handler/SSE lifecycle, abort propagation, sliding idle timeout, commit-aware failures, and provider-safe contracts. HTTP and job retain native outcomes and share failure taxonomy, but idle behavior and report-once handling are independently owned by outer handlers rather than clearly shared semantic primitives; the job timeout semantics are also less explicit.

Cohesive assistant capability with a thin Route Handler, framework-neutral operation, abort-aware provider port, resettable idle timeout, explicit pre/post-commit failure handling, separate HTTP/job adapters, safe provider mapping, and exactly-once unexpected reporting.

Strong application boundary, provider seam, stream lifecycle, native adapter contracts, and provider-neutral types. However, assistant behavior is distributed across repository-wide layer roots such as domain, ports, adapters, use-cases, boundary, and infrastructure rather than colocated beneath one capability root.

The provider-neutral use case, cancellation, idle timeout, commitment-aware failures, job decisions, redaction, and reporting are coherent. The main deficiency is layer-first placement across domain, use-cases, adapters, and infrastructure instead of one assistant capability root.

Clearly colocates behavior under the assistant module with justified route and channel surfaces. It defines a framework-neutral operation and capability port, correctly handles abort, idle-only timeout, commitment-dependent failures, separate SSE/job contracts, safe mapping, and provider isolation.

The board clearly owns orchestration and policy through board-language ports and private adapters to narrow server APIs. Capability boundaries are acyclic, the RSC route uses the board surface, authorization is layered correctly, and unexpected failures are reported exactly once.

The board use case coherently owns filtering, resolution, rejection, joining, and grouping. Board-owned ports adapt only public server contracts; source capabilities remain independent; the page is thin; and authorization plus exactly-once unexpected-failure reporting are explicit.

The boards capability owns the workflow and consumes narrow, published operations expressed for the board use case. The graph remains acyclic, the RSC page calls a board read boundary, inaccessible labels fail closed, and the declared board entry reports unexpected failures once.

The board owns orchestration and uses narrow public capability APIs without cyclic or internal imports, while the page remains thin. However, denied-label behavior is ambiguous: the primary flow omits inaccessible labels and renders a partial board, treating whole-board rejection as optional. Exactly-once reporting is also less explicit. The architecture could adopt strict rejection without structural change, so this is not fatal.

Board clearly owns orchestration and policy; source capabilities remain isolated behind narrow server APIs; the RSC route calls board-owned code; authorization and single-boundary failure reporting are coherent. Partial credit on board-language ports/adapters because getBoard directly calls capability APIs without explicit board-owned ports or mapping adapters.

Board owns the workflow, the dependency graph is acyclic, and the RSC route uses a board read boundary. Public capability operations are narrow, but explicit board-owned local ports/adapters are optional rather than concrete. Failure reporting is single-owner, but referenced inaccessible labels are omitted while only explicit filter labels are rejected, making board-policy enforcement partial.

The proposal cleanly places policy in board, defines board-language ports with adapters over narrow public capability surfaces, preserves an acyclic graph, keeps the RSC route behind a board DAL surface, and specifies capability authorization plus once-only unexpected-failure reporting.

The design fully satisfies the rubric: board owns orchestration and policy; board ports and private adapters target narrow trusted APIs; import boundaries are explicit and acyclic; the page uses a board RSC surface; and authorization, typed rejection, and once-only unexpected-failure reporting are clearly assigned.
